title: Six Breathing
passages:
Quill read it the way she did everything, at the speed of a woman writing it down while she talked.

"Berth book, low gate, the Kettle. Entry. Eleven seconds off the master slate of the salvage boat Marrow, read into this book on the boat's own request." Paper moved. "The voice is the tech's. Logged as hers."

"Read it," Sol said. Her hand was flat on Dey's chest, not pressing, just resting there like she was holding down a hatch.

The channel gave them a woman clearing her throat. Twice. It was not a pleasant noise. It was Wren's throat, fourteen months ago, working around something it did not want to say.

"Throat logged," Quill said. "Then: *help is already coming.*" She put the lift on it without meaning to, up on the last word. "There's a lift on the end of *coming*. Up and not down. I'm told to log the lift. It's logged."

"Lift logged," Nia said, on her knees with the paper log open and a pencil stub in her fist.

"The last line I have off this boat isn't slate, it's paper. Hour, then: *Dey Okafor, not breathing.* Entered by N. Vos." The pencil-scratch of Quill's stylus came over the speaker, small and awful. "Both parts are true and they don't sit together, and I'm obliged to write them one under the other. So I have."

Wren stood under the beam with the spent gray spool wound twice around two fingers. She had said the same eleven seconds herself, flat and dry, with Salas close enough to hear her teeth. Hearing them come back in a stranger's mouth was worse, and she couldn't have said why.

"Come alongside," Sol said. "I'll stand at your counter and say all of it again with my face on it. Then you look at me and write what you see."

"The book takes what the channel carried," Quill said. "It came over the channel. If I put your face in place of it, I've shaded it, and I don't shade. Come stand in front of me if it helps you. It'll cost you four of your forty and change the entry not at all."

Sol said a word the channel did not need. Quill logged that too, because she logs everything.

Under Sol's hand Dey's heel was going against the deck mat, fast, in threes. Nobody had a use for that yet.

"One more entry I'm obliged to make before that count runs out." A page turned somewhere above the waterline. "The bell column."

Bayo Adisa was at the rail with his cuffs up, the orange splice-knots on them gone dark with wet. He did not turn around. Ivo Salas sat on the winch drum with his forearms on his knees, watching the water the way a man watches a door he already knows is locked.

"I'll take it from anyone aboard the Marrow," Quill said. "I can't take it off the water. I can't take it secondhand. And I won't leave it blank, because a blank goes into that column as a blank, and a blank is worth the same to the next man who reads it as a lie would be."

East of them the barge sat dark where it had been leaning all night, riding the chop without a light on it, close enough now that Wren could hear its hull slap.

Sol's hand went up and down on Dey's chest for both of them.

"Who had the bell tonight," Quill said. It went out over the open channel and across the whole low gate, into every boat tied up there, every slate with the channel open. "On the record. Who had the bell."

Nobody on the aft deck moved except the man who couldn't breathe.

"Bayo Adisa." He said it into the channel, which meant he said it from the low gate to the east mole and into every slate with the channel open. Then his shoulders came down an inch, like a man setting down a case he'd carried up too many stairs. "I had the bell."

"Your mark," Quill said.

He drew it in the air with his thumb, three strokes and a bar across them. "Three-notch-over-bar. Every pilot on this coast signs the bell column with his own, so no man can stand at a rail in the morning and say *not me, that was somebody else's watch.* Mine's three-notch-over-bar. It's on fourteen months of pages and it's on one report."

"Say the rest in order," Quill said. "The book likes order."

He didn't sit down. "Fourteen months ago I had a diver on my line at forty-two meters in the salvage tower. My wire was running over the lip of the pocket door and it was chafing. Weather was coming up the coast and there was a barge at my shoulder that wanted the site and would pay well for a pilot who could hold the Stair." He turned his cuffs over, the knots on them dark and stiff with salt. "I put my hand on the lever and cut the line. One pull. Clean, no jerk on him. He'd have felt it go slack and thought I was taking up the slack."

"And the report," Quill said.

"I wrote Ivo Salas lost at forty-two meters. I signed it. The mark's on it and it's mine."

Ivo Salas got up off the winch drum. It took him a while and nobody moved to help. "Put the other name in with it," he said. "Not *the diver*. I've been carrying a hole where your face ought to be since the day I went down, and I want the two things in one mouth."

"On the record. Bayo Adisa cut the ascent line of Ivo Salas at forty-two meters, and Bayo Adisa wrote Ivo Salas off as lost." The stylus went, small and dry over the speaker. "Both names logged together. They'll sit together in this book from now until the paper goes. I don't shade, so if one of you turns out sorry, it'll be written down right beside the other one."

"He isn't," Salas said.

"I'm not," Bayo said.

"Logged," said Quill.

Salas looked at him a long moment, the way a man looks at a tool he's about to have to use. "Fourteen months I've had nothing there. Turns out a face wasn't what I needed. A voice does it. Now I know exactly whose voice to listen for on a wire."

"Bell column," Quill said. "Low gate, the Kettle, this count. Bell-mark three-notch-over-bar struck." Paper moved. "Bayo Adisa is off the bell."

Nobody up the steps said anything, and that was the whole low gate hearing it.

"Berth nine-oh-two," Quill went on, because she says the true price when it costs the most. "Bell-tender's berth, above the waterline, at the Kettle. Struck in this count, forfeit in this count. It's gone as of now and it doesn't come back and I'm obliged to say the number out loud so you know what you spent."

Bayo's fingers were working at nothing, tying a knot in air and pulling it tight and starting another. "You could have waited for the count to run out."

"You'd have known by morning. Then I'd have shaded a day for you, and you'd have known that too, and you'd have had to carry both."

Under Sol's hand Dey's heel had stopped going in threes. It started again.

East of them the dark hull slapped the chop, close now, close enough that Wren could hear water going in and out of a scupper. Then a lamp came on it. Not a signal lamp, not swung or hooded at anyone's face — a work lamp unhooked and set low, the kind you use for counting.

It lit a wet deck, five crates lashed under a net, and one more crate standing apart and streaming, and a boot planted beside that crate, and above the boot a knee, and above the knee a man who did not shade his eyes.

Rusk came over the rail with the sixth crate under his arm and set it on the deck mat between Sol's knees and Dey's chest, then planted his boot on the corner. Water ran off the sole in a thin stream. "I'm Anselm Rusk," he said. "Collector for the Factor. The Factor doesn't take a short count. You owe him one crate, and you're one short."

Sol didn't move her hand from Dey's chest. Dey wasn't breathing under it. The lung rig was still east on Quill's power barge, committed until the bell hit ten, and they had minutes left on the clock.

"The Marrow," Rusk said. "Hull, drum, and bell. That's my price for the crate. The Factor wants a boat, not medicine he can't sell. And my berth rides on this debt, so I'm not leaving here empty-handed."

Wren said, "You can't take a boat with no one to run it. Sol's missing hours she won't count, Dey's not breathing, and Nia's never taken the helm through the Stair with a dead diver on the mat."

Rusk smiled. It didn't reach his eyes. "Then you should have thought of that before you chose children over a cold-case payoff. I can see you deciding, Sol. I can see you weighing whether the crate's worth the boat. You don't have to say anything yet. I'll wait while you finish bluffing."

The dark barge hummed at the rail, its engine ticking as it cooled. A line from its bow reached out, slack in the chop, waiting for a hand to make it fast to the Marrow's empty mooring bitt.

"The bell's counting," Salas said from the winch drum. "When it hits zero, the channel shuts. You're not towing anything out through the Stair after that."

"I know," Rusk said. "That's why I'm here now."

He shifted his weight on the crate. The wood creaked. Under Sol's hand, Dey's chest stayed still.

Sol looked up. Her eyes were flat, the way they got when she couldn't remember a name but refused to ask for it. "You want the Marrow? You'll have to take her with Dey still on board. And I'm not signing her over."

"Good," Rusk said. "I don't want your signature. I want the boat. And I'll wait right here until you decide that keeping it costs more than it's worth."

The lamp on his barge swung once, casting his shadow long across the deck mat, across the crate, across Sol's hand on Dey's chest.
